citrus_black_spot.description: Fungal disease caused by Phyllosticta citricarpa. Thrives in warm, wet conditions.

high_humidity.description: Spore germination accelerates above 80% humidity. Wet leaves critical for infection.
high_humidity.action: Ensure canopy airflow. Remove wet debris. If fungicide not recently applied, apply copper or strobilurin before rain.

rainfall.description: Rain provides moisture for spore germination. Lesion development occurs 7-10 days post-infection.
rainfall.action: Apply fungicide preventatively before rain if humidity is high. Prune for better air circulation.

temperature.description: Disease develops slower below 20°C. Accelerates in warm seasons (summer).
temperature.action: Monitor closely during warm months. Increase fungicide frequency May-September.

leaf_wetness.description: Spores need 12+ hours of leaf wetness to infect. Morning dew or overhead irrigation increases risk.
leaf_wetness.action: Avoid overhead watering. Water at soil level early morning only. Remove standing water.

citrus_black_spot.critical_period: Spring through summer (petal fall through harvest)

citrus_canker.description: Bacterial disease (Xanthomonas citri subsp. citri). Spread by water splash and wind.

high_humidity.description: Humidity aids bacterial survival on leaf surfaces. Wind-blown water splash spreads bacteria.
high_humidity.action: Avoid overhead watering. Prune infected wood immediately. Disinfect tools.

rainfall.description: Rain + wind creates water droplets that spread bacteria to healthy tissue. High-speed winds increase spread.
rainfall.action: After rain, inspect for new lesions. If infection detected, prune affected branches immediately.

temperature.description: Bacterial growth and lesion expansion fastest at warm temperatures.
temperature.action: Monitor closely year-round but especially April-October. Apply copper bactericide preventatively.

wind_speed.description: Strong winds + rain create forceful water splash that disperses bacteria between trees.
wind_speed.action: Post-storm inspection critical. Increase spacing between trees. Remove infected trees if systemic.

citrus_canker.critical_period: Year-round, peaks in warm wet seasons

citrus_foliage_damage.description: Non-infectious leaf damage from pests (mites, leaf miners, scale) or fungal spotting.

high_temperature.description: Heat stress weakens plant defenses. Spider mites and scale insects reproduce faster in heat.
high_temperature.action: Increase irrigation to reduce stress. Apply horticultural oil in early morning or late evening (avoid heat).

low_humidity.description: Dry conditions stress foliage, making it more susceptible to pest damage.
low_humidity.action: Maintain consistent soil moisture. Increase misting frequency. Monitor for spider mites.

high_humidity.description: High humidity + warm temps = fungal leaf spots (Cercospora, etc.). Also favors scale insects.
high_humidity.action: Improve canopy airflow. Avoid wetting foliage. Apply copper fungicide if fungal spots appear.

prolonged_drought.description: Stress from drought reduces plant vigor and pest resistance.
prolonged_drought.action: Restore regular watering schedule. Improve soil moisture and nutrition.

citrus_greening.description: Bacterial disease (Candidatus Liberibacter) spread by Asian citrus psyllid vector. Incurable.

warm_temperature.description: Psyllid vector most active and reproduces fastest in warm weather (spring-fall).
warm_temperature.action: Monitor for psyllids year-round, intensify April-November. Use Imidacloprid during non-bloom periods.

high_humidity.description: High humidity favors psyllid nymphs. Adults more active in warm + humid conditions.
high_humidity.action: Scout for psyllids on new leaf flushes. Apply systemic insecticide if psyllids detected.

new_flush_growth.trigger: New leaves appearing after rain or fertilizer
new_flush_growth.description: Psyllids preferentially feed on new tender growth. Each new flush = feeding opportunity.
new_flush_growth.action: Time Imidacloprid sprays to protect new flushes. Avoid spraying during bloom.

rainfall.description: Rain stimulates new flush growth, which attracts psyllids.
rainfall.action: Within 2-3 days of rain triggering new growth, apply systemic insecticide if not blooming.

citrus_greening.monitoring_frequency: Every 3-4 days during warm months. Check new growth for psyllids.
citrus_greening.note: No cure exists. Prevention through psyllid control is only option. Confirm diagnosis with agricultural extension before removing tree.

citrus_healthy.description: Healthy foliage and fruit. No disease present.

citrus_melanose.description: Fungal disease (Diaporthe citri). Infects dead wood and spreads to fruit/leaves via splash.

rainfall.description: Rain creates spore-laden water splash from infected dead wood to healthy fruit/leaves.
rainfall.action: Prune dead wood before rainy season. If disease present, apply copper fungicide during fruit development.

temperature.description: Disease development fastest during early fruit development phase (spring into early summer).
temperature.action: Prune dead wood in late winter. Apply fungicide March-June during early fruit development.

high_temperature.description: Copper fungicides lose efficacy above 32°C. Application timing critical.
high_temperature.action: Apply copper fungicide early morning or late evening when temps below 32°C.

humidity.description: Spore germination accelerates in humid conditions.
humidity.action: Ensure canopy airflow. Remove dead wood which harbors spores.

citrus_melanose.monitoring_frequency: Every 2 weeks March-June. Inspect fruit and foliage.

mango_anthracnose.description: Fungal disease (Colletotrichum gloeosporioides). Thrives in warm, wet conditions.

rainfall.description: Spores splash-dispersed during rain. Infection occurs within 12-24 hours of rain on young fruit/flowers.
rainfall.action: Remove infected debris immediately. Spray Mancozeb or copper every 10-14 days during wet weather.

high_humidity.description: Disease accelerates in humid conditions. Conidiospores germinate rapidly above 85% RH.
high_humidity.action: Improve canopy airflow. Avoid overhead watering. Apply fungicide preventatively before wet season.

warm_temperature.description: Fungus grows fastest at 24-28°C. Infection occurs faster at warm temps.
warm_temperature.action: Monitor closely during warm wet months. Increase fungicide frequency May-September.

flowering_period.description: Flowers and young fruitlets are highly susceptible. Infection during bloom stage causes fruit drop.
flowering_period.action: Start fungicide spray program at flower bud stage. Maintain 10-14 day intervals through fruit set.

mango_anthracnose.critical_period: Flowering through fruit development (March-June in most regions)
mango_anthracnose.monitoring_frequency: Every 5-7 days during flowering and wet season

mango_bacterial_canker.description: Bacterial disease (Xanthomonas campestris pv. mangiferaeindicae). Spread by water and tools.

rainfall.description: Rain with wind spreads bacteria via water splash. Infection occurs through wounds or stomata.
rainfall.action: Avoid overhead watering. Prune infected branches immediately after rain.

high_humidity.description: High humidity aids bacterial survival. Stomatal opening increases during humid conditions.
high_humidity.action: Improve air circulation. Disinfect pruning tools with 70% alcohol between cuts.

temperature.description: Bacteria most active in warm weather. Lesion expansion fastest at 25-30°C.
temperature.action: Monitor closely year-round but especially warm months. Apply copper bactericide to new growth.

wind_damage.description: Wind-driven rain creates wounds where bacteria enter. Branch breakage from wind = infection pathway.
wind_damage.action: After storms, inspect for broken branches. Prune infected wood immediately. Apply bactericide to wounds.

mango_bacterial_canker.critical_period: Year-round, peaks during warm wet season

mango_cutting_weevil.description: Insect pest (Sternochetus weakly). Larvae tunnel in shoots, causing wilting and dieback.

warm_temperature.description: Adult weevil activity and reproduction increases above 20°C.
warm_temperature.action: Monitor new shoots from spring onward. Collect and burn infested shoots.

rainfall.description: Rain triggers new shoot growth, which attracts laying females.
rainfall.action: Scout for new shoot damage 1-2 weeks after rain. Remove infested shoots immediately.

new_flush_growth.description: Females lay eggs on tender new growth. Larvae burrow into shoots causing wilting.
new_flush_growth.action: Check new shoots weekly during growing season. Prune infested shoots 10cm below damage.

moderate_humidity.description: Pest activity optimal in moderate humidity during warm season.
moderate_humidity.action: Monitor shoots weekly spring-summer. Use Spinosad only if severe and not blooming.

mango_cutting_weevil.note: Only apply insecticide if infestation is severe and trees not in bloom.

mango_die_back.description: Fungal disease (Lasiodiplodia or Botryodiplodia). Infects branch ends and spreads downward.

drought_stress.description: Drought weakens tree vigor. Fungus enters through branch tips and spreads when tree is stressed.
drought_stress.action: Restore regular watering. Prune 10cm below diseased wood. Disinfect tools between cuts.

high_temperature.description: Heat + drought stress = optimal conditions for dieback fungus to kill branch tips.
high_temperature.action: Improve irrigation to reduce stress. Prune affected branches. Apply fungicide to wounds.

rainfall.description: Rain after drought stress can trigger disease expansion if branches already infected.
rainfall.action: Prune diseased branches before rainy season. Apply Carbendazim or copper to wounds.

temperature_fluctuation.description: Rapid temperature changes stress branches and allow fungal entry.
temperature_fluctuation.action: Monitor for branch damage during temperature swings. Prune promptly if dieback detected.

mango_die_back.critical_period: Dry season (drought risk) and temperature transition seasons
mango_die_back.monitoring_frequency: Every 2 weeks during dry season. Inspect branch ends.

mango_gall_midge.description: Insect pest (Procontarinia mataniensis). Larvae cause leaf gall formation and stunting.

rainfall.description: Rain stimulates new leaf flush, which attracts egg-laying females. Peak midge activity post-rain.
rainfall.action: Scout new flushes 3-5 days after rain. Remove galled leaves immediately to prevent spread.

warm_temperature.description: Midge development, flight, and egg-laying fastest in warm weather (spring-summer).
warm_temperature.action: Monitor intensively April-September. Apply systemic insecticide during early flush stage.

high_humidity.description: Eggs and larvae thrive in humid microenvironments within galls.
high_humidity.action: Improve canopy airflow. Remove infested leaves to disrupt midge life cycle.

new_flush_growth.description: Females lay eggs on tender new growth. Larvae create galls as leaves expand.
new_flush_growth.action: Apply systemic insecticide (Imidacloprid) at early flush stage. Repeat in 2 weeks if needed.

mango_gall_midge.critical_period: Spring through early summer (new flush periods)
mango_gall_midge.note: Early detection and leaf removal critical. Systemic insecticide most effective.

mango_healthy.description: Healthy mango foliage and fruit. No disease or pest pressure detected.

mango_powdery_mildew.description: Fungal disease (Oidium mangiferae). Spreads via spores. Does not require free water.

warm_dry_climate.description: Powdery mildew UNIQUE: thrives in warm, DRY conditions (opposite of most fungi). Spores spread via air currents.
warm_dry_climate.action: Do NOT increase humidity. Remove infected panicles. Spray sulfur or potassium bicarbonate every 7-10 days.

flowering_period.description: Panicles (flower clusters) highly susceptible. Infection reduces fruit set.
flowering_period.action: Start fungicide spray at panicle emergence. Maintain 7-10 day intervals through bloom.

light_rainfall.description: Unlike most fungi, wetting can help sulfur fungicides adhere. But excessive water washes spores.
light_rainfall.action: Spray sulfur early morning when conditions are cool and dry. Do not spray sulfur with oil.

high_temperature.description: Disease slows above 30°C. Sulfur sprays less effective in extreme heat.
high_temperature.action: Spray in early morning or late afternoon. Avoid midday heat.

mango_powdery_mildew.critical_period: Flowering period (variable by region, typically 2-3 months)
mango_powdery_mildew.note: Sulfur very effective but do NOT mix with oil. Potassium bicarbonate also works.

mango_sooty_mould.description: Fungal disease (Capnodium/Scorias species). Secondary — grows on honeydew from pests (aphids, scale, whitefly).

high_humidity.description: Sooty mould fungus thrives in humid conditions. Also favors pest survival (scale, aphids produce more honeydew).
high_humidity.action: Treat underlying pests with neem oil. Improve canopy airflow to reduce humidity.

rainfall.description: Rain can wash away sooty mould temporarily, but pests (aphids/scale) often increase post-rain.
rainfall.action: Scout for pests after rain. If pests found, apply neem oil. Wash leaves with mild soap.

warm_temperature.description: Pest activity (aphids/scale) highest in warm months. Sooty mould follows pest presence.
warm_temperature.action: Monitor for pests year-round, intensify April-October. Treat pests with neem oil preventatively.

low_leaf_wetness.description: Sooty mould persists and accumulates on leaf surfaces. Does not require water to survive.
low_leaf_wetness.action: Once pests controlled, wash leaves with mild soap to restore photosynthesis.

mango_sooty_mould.monitoring_frequency: Every 5-7 days during warm months. Scout for underlying pests.
mango_sooty_mould.note: Sooty mould is symptom of pest infestation, not primary disease. Treat the pests (aphids/scale), not the mould directly.
